tier_reason: First-party console output with public harnesses (test_stb_xml.c, test_libxml.c) and gcc -O2 flags, but no CPU model. The headline 1MB figure is a harness artifact, so the result is capped at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Small 72B XML: 188 MB/s vs libxml2 15 MB/s ~12.5x; medium ~1KB XML: 556 MB/s vs 36 MB/s ~15x (derived from page data). The 1MB figure (8707 MB/s vs 46 MB/s, ~189x; README claims 193x) is invalid: run_parser caps xml_parse at 10000 tokens, so stb_xml stops early (10000 tokens vs 87357 nodes libxml2 builds) while MB/s is computed over the full 1,048,653 bytes.
corrections.workload: Parse synthetic small (72B), medium (~1KB), and generated large (~1MB) XML, timed with clock() over 10 to 100000 iterations. stb_xml is a tokenizer (test_stb_xml.c, 10000-token buffer); libxml2 uses xmlParseMemory plus xmlFreeDoc, building a full DOM (test_libxml.c).
corrections.caveats: In test_stb_xml.c, run_parser passes max_tokens=10000, and xml_parse stops at token_count < max_tokens. On the 1MB file only about the first 10000 tokens are tokenized, yet throughput is computed over the whole file, so the 189x/193x claim is overstated by roughly an order of magnitude. The two sides do different work: tokenize-only, with minimal error checking, vs a full DOM build. The libxml2 side is a system shared library with its build flags unknown. No CPU model is given. The repo is 2 commits on 2026-01-05, with 2 stars.

notes: The 1MB throughput number is a measurement bug (token cap), not a real speedup. The only defensible numbers are the ~12-15x small and medium cases, which are still tokenizer vs DOM. The record said xmlReadMemory; the code uses xmlParseMemory. Metadata checks out: BSD-3-Clause, 2 stars, last commit 2026-01-05. The orchestrator may want to drop it as not notable.
